parts.title: Task 1 · Long reading: choose a title for each paragraph
parts.instruction: Read the article about a village shop. It has five paragraphs, numbered 1 to 5. Choose the best title (a to f) for each paragraph (questions 1 to 5). Each title can be used only once, and one title is not needed. Task 1 should take about 20 minutes. You have 120 minutes for Reading and Writing together.

pool.b: A big supermarket opens in Harnford
pool.c: Why the village needed a shop
pool.d: Costs, profit and advice for others
pool.f: Who works there and what it sells

texts.label: Task 1
texts.title: The shop that the village built
paras: [1] When the last shop in the Devon village of Harnford closed in 2016, residents lost more than a place to buy milk. The nearest supermarket was eleven miles away, and the bus ran only twice a day. “People who didn't drive simply stopped eating fresh food,” says Priya Nair, a retired nurse. Within a year, she and a group of neighbours had decided to do something about it.

[2] Rather than look for a single owner, the group offered shares in the shop at £10 each. Nobody was allowed to buy more than 200 shares, so that no one person could take control. Within four months, 312 residents had bought shares and raised £94,000. A grant of £30,000 from a lottery fund then covered the cost of buying the empty building and fitting it out.

[3] Today the shop employs a full-time manager, Tom Achebe, and two part-time assistants. Around 40 volunteers cover the rest of the opening hours, working three-hour shifts. About a third of the stock comes from farms and small producers within 15 miles, including eggs, cheese and bread from a bakery in the next valley. Prices are higher than in the supermarket for most everyday items, Achebe admits. “We can't compete on baked beans,” he says. “But customers know where their money goes, and they seem happy to pay a little extra for that.”

[4] The shop has become a meeting point as well as a place to buy food. A post office counter operates on two mornings a week, and a coffee morning every Friday attracts about 25 people, many of them elderly residents who live alone. On Thursdays, volunteers deliver orders to neighbours who cannot leave their homes. “Some of them used to see nobody all week,” Nair says. “Now they see at least one friendly face.”

[5] Running a community shop is not easy. Refrigeration is expensive, so last year solar panels were fitted on the roof, which has cut electricity costs by about a quarter. The volunteers are getting older, too, and finding younger helpers is a constant worry. Even so, the shop made a profit of £6,200 last year, which goes into a fund for village projects. The Harnford group has also advised seven other villages that want to follow its example, and Nair is optimistic. “If a shop run by retired teachers and part-time gardeners can survive, so can yours,” she tells them.

parts.title: Task 2 · Multi-text reading: which text?
parts.instruction: Read the four texts, A to D, about a trial in the town of Aldbury. For questions 19 to 23, decide which text each question refers to. You can use a text more than once. Task 2 should take about 20 minutes.

texts.label: Text A
texts.title: Cars off the High Street: trial begins in Aldbury
paras: From the first Saturday in June, private cars will be banned from Aldbury High Street between 10 am and 5 pm. The six-month trial, approved by the town council by nine votes to five, will cost £48,000, mostly for removable barriers and new signs. Buses, taxis and cyclists may still use the street, and drivers with a disabled badge will be allowed to park in two marked bays.

Councillor Rosa Delgado says the aim is to make the town centre “a place people want to stay in, not just drive through”. Pedestrian counts will be taken every Saturday, and the results will be published on the council website. If the trial is a success, the ban could be extended to Sundays next year.

texts.label: Text B
texts.title: From Hannah Okafor, owner of Okafor Books, to the Aldbury Traders' Association
paras: Dear all, I want to be fair: I'm not against the idea of a car-free High Street. But Saturday is my busiest day, and it brings in almost a third of my weekly takings. Many of my customers come from villages where there is no bus on Saturdays, and they leave with heavy bags of books.

I'd have preferred the council to try the ban on a quieter day first, say a Tuesday. I have also asked for a free shuttle from the Mill Lane car park, but I haven't had a reply. If our takings fall by more than 10 per cent in the first month, I will ask everyone here to sign a petition to end the trial. Best wishes, Hannah

texts.label: Text C
texts.title: Letter to the editor from Ibrahim Khalil
paras: I am 78 and walk with a stick, so the news about the High Street made me nervous. Until now I have driven in every Saturday to meet friends for coffee. The two bays for badge holders are at the far end of the street, 300 metres from the chemist, and that is a long way when your legs are tired.

I am not saying the idea is wrong. In fact, I would welcome the trial if the council put a bench every fifty metres, so that people like me could rest. I imagine my grandchildren would love a street where they can walk about without worrying about traffic.

texts.label: Text D
texts.title: Aldbury Families Group: newsletter
paras: We asked 400 local parents about the High Street. A clear 71 per cent told us they avoid it at weekends because of the traffic and the narrow pavements. That is why we back the car-free Saturdays.

On the first Saturday of the trial, our volunteers will run chalk drawing and music for children in the middle of the street. We would also like to see more places to leave bicycles: at the moment there are only six cycle racks on the whole street.

items.prompt: Which text says how much the trial will cost?
Which text suggests trying the ban on a different day of the week?
Which text asks for places to sit down?
Which text reports the results of a survey?
Which text mentions that people might sign a petition against the trial?

parts.title: Task 3 · Reading into writing
parts.instruction: Use the information in all four Task 2 texts (A to D) to write 150 to 180 words. Use your own words: do not copy whole sentences from the texts. Organise your answer clearly and give your own recommendation. Task 3 should take about 40 minutes. Reading and Writing share one 120-minute clock.

tasks.title: Task 3 · Report on the Aldbury High Street trial
tasks.situation: The four Task 2 texts are about a six-month trial in the town of Aldbury. Text A, a news report: private cars are banned from the High Street on Saturdays from 10 am to 5 pm; the trial costs £48,000; buses, taxis and cyclists are still allowed, and disabled badge holders may park in two bays. Text B, an email from bookshop owner Hannah Okafor: she is not against the idea, but Saturday brings in almost a third of her weekly takings; she wants a free shuttle from the Mill Lane car park and would petition against the trial if takings fall by more than 10 per cent in the first month. Text C, a letter from 78-year-old Ibrahim Khalil: the disabled bays are 300 metres from the chemist; he would welcome the trial with a bench every fifty metres. Text D, a newsletter from the Families Group: 71 per cent of 400 parents avoid the High Street at weekends because of traffic; they back the trial but want more cycle racks (there are six).
tasks.prompt: You work for the town council. Write a short report for the councillors that summarises the main views in the four texts and recommends what the council should do next.
points: Say briefly what the trial is.
Summarise what the supporters and the worried residents say.
Recommend what the council should do next, and give a reason.
Use your own words and a clear report structure.
tasks.model:
Subject: Views on the High Street trial

This report summarises four opinions on the car-free Saturday trial in Aldbury.

The council has approved a six-month ban on private cars between 10 am and 5 pm, costing £48,000. Buses, taxis and cyclists may still use the street, and badge holders can park in two bays. The Families Group strongly supports the idea: 71 per cent of the parents it asked avoid the High Street at weekends because of traffic. However, other residents have worries. Ibrahim Khalil, who walks with a stick, says the disabled bays are 300 metres from the chemist and wants benches. Hannah Okafor, a bookseller, brings in nearly a third of her weekly income on Saturdays and fears losing customers from villages without buses.

I would recommend keeping the trial but adding benches, a free shuttle from Mill Lane car park and more cycle racks. The council should also review shop takings after the first month. That would show whether the benefits for walkers outweigh the costs to traders.
checklist: Task fulfilment: you cover the trial, the views of supporters and of worried residents, and you make a clear recommendation. 150 to 180 words.
Reading for writing: you use information from all four texts (A, B, C and D), selected and combined in your own words rather than copied.
Organisation and structure: a heading or subject line, a short introduction, clear paragraphs and linking words (however, on the other hand, therefore).
Language control: a suitably formal, neutral register; accurate B2 grammar (reporting verbs, conditionals, linking); vocabulary such as takings, badge holders, trial.
Check the word count: more than 180 words or fewer than 150 can lose marks.

parts.title: Task 4 · Extended writing
parts.instruction: Write an article of 150 to 180 words on the topic below. Give your own opinion and support it with reasons and examples. Task 4 should take about 40 minutes.

tasks.title: Task 4 · Article: working from home
tasks.situation: Your college careers website is running a series called “The world of work today”. Many employees now work from home for part or all of the week. The editor has asked readers to send in short articles.
tasks.prompt: Write an article for the website: Is working from home a good thing for most people? Discuss the advantages and the disadvantages and say what you think is the best solution.
points: Give two or three advantages of working from home.
Say what you think is the best solution, and why.
Use a title, clear paragraphs and linking words.
tasks.model:
Working from home: a blessing or a trap?

Since remote work became common, the question is whether it really suits everyone. In my experience, the answer is both yes and no.

The advantages are obvious. You save time and money on commuting, and you can organise your day around your own needs. I have more energy for my family because I no longer spend two hours a day on trains. Many employers also report that staff concentrate better without constant interruptions.

On the other hand, working at home has disadvantages. It can be lonely, especially for people who live alone, and it is surprisingly difficult to switch off when your desk is in the living room. Younger employees may also miss the chance to learn from more experienced colleagues.

In my opinion, the best solution is a mixture: two or three days at home and the rest in the office. That way people enjoy flexibility without losing contact with their team. Companies should let employees choose what suits them.
checklist: Task fulfilment: advantages, disadvantages and your own conclusion are all covered, with reasons and examples. 150 to 180 words.
Organisation and structure: a title, an introduction, one paragraph per main idea, a conclusion, and linking words (on the other hand, in my opinion, that way).
Register: an engaging but fairly neutral style that suits a website article for adult readers.
Language control: a range of B2 structures (comparatives, relative clauses, conditionals, passive) and accurate spelling and punctuation.
Keep to the word limit and leave a minute to check your text.

parts.title: Independent listening · first listening: what is it about?
parts.instruction: You will hear a radio discussion once. In the exam, you would tell the examiner in one or two sentences what the talk is about. Here, choose the best answer (question 1).

clips.title: Radio discussion: mobile phones in schools

script.t: Good morning, and welcome to Morning Debate. Today we're asking whether schools should ban mobile phones during the school day. More and more head teachers say yes, but not everyone agrees. With me are Daniel Whitfield, head teacher of a secondary school in Leeds, and Dr Amara Osei, who researches how teenagers use technology.
Daniel, your school introduced a ban two years ago. Why?

Honestly, because break times had become silent. Pupils were sitting in rows, staring at screens instead of talking to each other. And teachers were spending a lot of every lesson telling children to put their phones away. Now pupils lock their phones in their bags at the start of the day. Lessons run much more smoothly, and what surprised me is that pupils say they feel less anxious, because they're no longer checking what everyone else is posting. Some parents were worried at first, because they wanted to be able to reach their children in an emergency. So we told them to phone the school office, and that has worked well.
Amara, do you agree with that approach?

I understand why schools do it, but I'm not sure a complete ban is the answer. The evidence is mixed. Some studies find a small improvement in test results, mainly for pupils who usually struggle, but very little difference for everyone else. My worry is that a ban doesn't teach anything. These young people will use phones all their lives, so it would be better to teach them how to manage them, to decide for themselves when to put the phone away. And phones can be useful in class, for research or for translating a word. A blanket ban throws that away.
We did try managed use first, Amara, and it didn't work. Teachers can't be police officers. And I'd argue that pupils learn self-control precisely because the phone is out of reach for six hours.
Perhaps. But does it carry over to home? In one study I worked on, pupils at schools with a ban spent just as long on their phones in the evening as everybody else.
So where does that leave us? Daniel, last word.
Whatever a school decides, it should talk to pupils and parents first. We held meetings for a whole term before we introduced our rule, and that made all the difference.
I'd completely agree with that. Consulting people is the one thing every school should do, whatever the rule is.

items.question: What is the discussion mainly about?
options: How teenagers can be kept safe on social media.
Whether schools should stop pupils using mobile phones.
Why pupils' test results have fallen in recent years.

options: Pupils had stopped talking to each other at break.
Parents had complained about phone use.

items.question: How does the school deal with parents who want to contact their children?
options: Pupils may send them a message at lunchtime.
Pupils may keep their phones switched on in their bags.
Parents can phone the school office.

items.question: What does Dr Osei say about the evidence on phone bans?
options: Test results improve a little, mainly for pupils who usually struggle.
Test results improve a great deal for all pupils.
Bans have no effect on test results at all.

options: Ban phones for the whole day, as Daniel's school has done.
Teach pupils to manage their own phone use.
Let pupils use their phones whenever they like.

items.question: What do both speakers agree on at the end?
options: Schools should consult pupils and parents before deciding.
Parents should take phones away from their children at home.
Phones should also be banned in primary schools.

parts.title: Topic
parts.instruction: Speak to the examiner for up to 4 minutes about a topic you have prepared. Choose a topic you can discuss in detail, plan four or five points (a mind map or short notes is fine) and bring them with you. The examiner will ask you questions about what you say. This practice task shows a sample topic and how to prepare it.

tasks.title: Topic · Volunteering in my community (sample)
tasks.situation: In the exam you choose your own topic (for example a hobby, a place, a social issue or an experience) and tell the examiner in advance. Here is a sample mind map. Prepare your own topic in the same way: four or five points, a few key words for each, one example or personal story per point, and an opinion. Practise speaking for about two minutes, then expect questions.

card.title: Sample mind map: Volunteering in my community
lines: 1. What volunteering is and who does it
3. My own experience (a food bank, a sports club, a charity shop)
5. Should schools ask students to volunteer?

redemittel: The topic I've chosen is …
First of all, I'd like to explain what … means.
One of the main reasons why people … is that …
From my own experience, I can say that …
On the one hand … on the other hand …
As far as I'm concerned, … / In my view, …
That's a good question. I suppose it depends on …
tasks.model:
Candidate: The topic I've chosen is volunteering in my community. First of all, volunteering means giving your time without being paid, for example at a food bank or a youth club. In my town, it's mostly retired people and students who do it. People volunteer for different reasons: some want to help, others want to meet people or add something to their CV. I've been helping at a food bank for about a year, every second Saturday. It's tiring, but it's rewarding to see how grateful families are. The advantages are obvious: you learn new skills and feel part of a community. The main disadvantage is that it takes time, and not everybody can afford to work for free. As far as I'm concerned, schools should encourage students to volunteer, but they shouldn't force them.
Examiner: Do you think volunteering can replace paid work in some areas?
Candidate: I don't think so. Volunteers are a wonderful addition, but important services such as hospitals or care homes need trained, paid staff. If we relied on volunteers too much, standards could fall.
Examiner: What would you say to someone who has never volunteered?
Candidate: I'd suggest starting small, perhaps just one afternoon a month, so that they can see whether they enjoy it.
checklist: Communicative effectiveness: you talk about all four or five points, give reasons and examples, and develop your opinions rather than just listing facts.
Interactive listening: you understand the examiner's questions, answer them fully and, if needed, ask for repetition politely.
Language control: a range of B2 structures and vocabulary, with errors that do not get in the way of meaning.
Delivery: clear pronunciation, natural rhythm, and you speak from notes rather than reading them out.

parts.title: Collaborative
parts.instruction: The examiner reads out a short problem. Ask questions to find out more, comment on what you hear, offer advice and keep the conversation going. You have up to 4 minutes. You do not prepare this part: you respond to what the examiner says.

tasks.title: Collaborative · A noisy neighbour
tasks.situation: The examiner says: “I'm having a problem with my neighbour. Her dog barks all day while she's at work, and it's driving me mad. I've never spoken to her, and I don't know whether to knock on her door, leave her a note or complain to the landlord. I really don't know what to do.” Ask questions, give your opinion and advice, and keep the conversation going.

card.title: What you can do
lines: Ask questions to find out more (how long, how often, what you have tried).
Comment on what the examiner says (that sounds stressful).
Give advice and say why it might work.
Keep the conversation going: ask what the examiner thinks of your ideas.

redemittel: How long has this been going on?
Have you thought about …?
That sounds really stressful.
If I were you, I'd … because …
She might not even realise that …
What do you think would happen if …?
Do you think that would help, or would it make things worse?
tasks.model:
Examiner: I'm having a problem with my neighbour. Her dog barks all day while she's at work. I don't know whether to knock on her door, leave her a note or complain to the landlord.
Candidate: That sounds really stressful. How long has this been going on?
Examiner: For about three months now.
Candidate: That's a long time. Have you ever spoken to her, or does she know that it bothers you?
Examiner: No, I've never spoken to her.
Candidate: Then she might not even realise there's a problem, because she's out all day. If I were you, I'd start by writing a friendly note, because that's less confrontational than knocking on her door.
Examiner: But what if she ignores it?
Candidate: That's possible. In that case, you could try speaking to her in person. People often react better when they meet you face to face. And if that doesn't work, going to the landlord would be the next step. Do you get on with the other neighbours?
Examiner: Yes, quite well.
Candidate: Then perhaps you could ask them whether the barking bothers them too. If several people complain, it's harder to ignore. What do you think about that idea?
Examiner: Good idea. Thanks.
checklist: Communicative effectiveness: you ask relevant questions, react to the answers and give clear advice with reasons.
Interactive listening: you use what the examiner says in your next turn (in that case, then, so) instead of preparing separate speeches.
Language control: B2 functions such as advising, speculating, eliciting information and comparing options, with accurate conditionals and modal verbs.
Delivery: friendly, supportive intonation, and no long pauses; you keep the conversation moving.

parts.title: Conversation
parts.instruction: The examiner chooses one subject area and starts a conversation with you for about 2 minutes. The subject areas are: society and living standards, personal values and ideals, the world of work, national environmental concerns, and public figures past and present. Give full answers with reasons and examples, and be ready to explain your opinions.

tasks.title: Conversation · The world of work (sample)
tasks.situation: The examiner has chosen the subject area “the world of work” and asks you about it. Your answers should be longer than one sentence: give an opinion, a reason and, where you can, an example.

card.title: Examiner's questions
lines: Do you think people today are under more pressure at work than in the past?
How important is it to enjoy your job, compared with earning a good salary?
Some people say that you should stay in one job for many years. What do you think?

redemittel: I'd say that … because …
It depends on …
Personally, I think … although …
For example, a friend of mine …
Compared with the past, …
That's partly true, but …
tasks.model:
Examiner: Do you think people today are under more pressure at work than in the past?
Candidate: I'd say yes, in some ways. Because of email and smartphones, it's difficult to switch off. A friend of mine answers messages from her boss in the evenings. On the other hand, working conditions are better in many ways, for example there is more flexibility.
Examiner: How important is it to enjoy your job, compared with earning a good salary?
Candidate: Personally, I think enjoying your job matters more in the long run. A high salary is nice, but if you dislike what you do, you'll probably be unhappy. Of course, it depends on your situation: if you have a family to support, money may be the priority.
Examiner: Some people say that you should stay in one job for many years. What do you think?
Candidate: That's partly true, because you build up experience. But I think changing jobs can be a good way to learn new skills, so I wouldn't say there is one right answer.
checklist: Communicative effectiveness: each answer contains an opinion, a reason and, where possible, an example; you do not stop after one sentence.
Interactive listening: you answer the question you were asked and react naturally to follow-up questions.
Language control: appropriate B2 vocabulary for work and society, and a mix of simple and complex sentences.
Delivery: clear and natural; do not rush, as you have only about two minutes.
